setup: This story opens before there are any Hittites at all. The central Anatolian plateau — modern Turkey, a high, cold, treeless steppe ringed by mountains — is already a working civilization, and has been for over a thousand years. The people there are the Hattians, who speak a language unrelated to anything else on earth, build fortified towns, and bury their elite with gold sun discs and bronze stags at places like Alaca Höyük. By around 1950 BCE merchants from Assur in Mesopotamia have laced the region with trading colonies, the largest at Kanesh, and they bring with them a technology that will change everything: cuneiform writing. What this chapter is really setting up is a substitution. Somewhere in this world, Indo-European speakers — distant linguistic cousins of the future Greeks and Romans — are quietly moving from being one population among many to being the ruling class, and they will absorb the Hattian world so completely that they take its name. The drama isn't a conquest. It's a question of who was already here, and how much of them survives inside the people who replaced them.

bridge: Chapter 1 left us with the ingredients but not the empire: a Hattian cultural foundation of metalwork, gods, and fortified towns; an international trade network running cuneiform and tin through colonies like Kanesh; and a new Indo-European-speaking ruling class quietly settling into central Anatolia, already showing up in the records under names like Anitta. By roughly 1750 BCE the stage is set. Someone is about to take all of it and build something — but first someone has to burn it down.
setup: This chapter is about how the Hittite Old Kingdom got founded, and why it could never stop tearing itself apart. King Anitta of Kussara conquers the city of Hattusa, levels it, and curses anyone who rebuilds it. About a century later Hattusili I rebuilds it anyway, makes it his capital, and starts conquering south into Syria. His grandson Mursili I pulls off one of the most audacious raids in ancient history — marching 600 miles to sack Babylon itself. But the same dynasty that conquers abroad murders itself at home: with no fixed rule for who inherits the throne and a noble assembly (the panku) expecting a say, nearly every succession becomes a potential assassination. Three kings die violently in a row, each killed by the next. What's at stake is whether this brilliant, expansionist kingdom can solve the one problem its own structure keeps creating — and the man who finally tries to fix it does so not with an army but with a written law.

bridge: After Telipinu's succession reform in Chapter 2 slowed the assassinations, the Hittite kingdom slid into a poorly documented slump — the Middle Hittite Period — squeezed by Kaska raiders from the north and the powerful Hurrian kingdom of Mitanni from the southeast, losing the Syrian territory Hattusili I and Mursili I had won. On the world stage this is the age of Egypt's New Kingdom and an interconnected club of great powers trading and fighting over Syria. The Hittites are barely hanging on at the edge of that club. Then one king drags them back into it — and past everyone else in it.
setup: This chapter is the hinge of the whole story: Suppiluliuma I, the greatest king the Hittites ever produced. In a single generation he rebuilds the army, destroys the rival superpower Mitanni, plants his own sons on Syrian thrones, and starts writing to the pharaoh of Egypt as an equal — "Brother" to "Brother" — in the diplomatic world of the Amarna Letters. Then comes the strangest episode in Bronze Age history: an Egyptian queen, newly widowed and afraid, writes begging him to send one of his sons to become her husband and pharaoh of Egypt. Nothing like it had ever happened. Suppiluliuma sends a son. The son is murdered on the road. The retaliation that follows brings home Egyptian prisoners — and a plague that will kill Suppiluliuma himself and ravage the empire for twenty years. What's at stake is whether the superpower he built can survive the catastrophe he accidentally unleashed.

bridge: The political story has run from foundation through near-collapse: by Suppiluliuma I and his son Mursili II (Chapter 3), the Hittites are a superpower that corresponds with Egypt as an equal, even as a twenty-year plague tears through them. Along the way they have been absorbing not just territory but gods — Hattian ones from the people they replaced, Hurrian ones flowing in through the southeastern kingdom of Kizzuwatna. This chapter steps out of the war-and-succession narrative to look at the strangest thing the Hittites built: a religion designed to never say no to a new god.
setup: The Hittite state worshipped what its own texts call the "Thousand Gods of Hatti," and that was not really an exaggeration. Where Egypt and Mesopotamia kept tidy ranked pantheons, the Hittites collected deities the way some institutions collect honorary degrees: every conquered or allied people's gods got added to the roster, given a temple, and invited to the festivals. Their archive holds ritual texts in at least eight languages. At the top stand the Storm God of Hatti and the Sun Goddess of Arinna — who is, strikingly, his equal or superior, mirrored on earth by the unusually powerful office of the queen, the Tawananna. This chapter explains why a civilization would build a religion this sprawling and inclusive, what it borrowed (a Hurrian myth that may be the direct ancestor of Greek mythology), and what it carved into the living rock at the sanctuary of Yazılıkaya. The Hittites weren't being tolerant for tolerance's sake — they were running a divine insurance policy, and the logic of it explains a great deal about how they ruled.

bridge: Chapter 4 stepped aside to map the Hittites' thousand-god religious world; now the political collision the whole story has been building toward arrives. Two superpowers have been circling each other for decades — the Hittite Empire, dominant in Syria since Suppiluliuma I (Chapter 3), and Egypt, eager to win back the Syrian territory it had lost. Both claim the same wealthy corridor of trade cities. Both know the circling has to end. Around 1295 BCE a new Hittite king, Muwatalli II, takes the throne and makes a provocative move — shifting the capital south toward the front — while a young, ambitious pharaoh prepares to march north and take Syria back.
setup: This chapter is the Hittites' two most famous moments, back to back. First comes the Battle of Kadesh in 1274 BCE, the largest chariot battle in ancient history — Muwatalli II's heavier three-man Hittite chariots against Ramesses II's faster two-man Egyptian ones, fought through a brilliant Hittite ambush and a near-disaster that both sides would carve onto their walls as a personal triumph. (Both lied; it was a draw.) Then comes the part that actually mattered. After Kadesh, the Hittite throne is seized in a coup by Hattusili III, who has to write the oldest political autobiography in history to justify it. And it's this usurper who, around 1259 BCE, negotiates with Ramesses II the document the Hittites are most remembered for: the world's first known peace treaty between equals — co-signed by his formidable queen, Puduhepa, and so durable a copy hangs in the United Nations today. What's at stake is whether two empires that fought the biggest battle of the age can do something genuinely new: choose to stop.

bridge: Chapters 3 through 5 showed the Hittites at their height — destroying Mitanni, fighting Egypt to a draw at Kadesh, and signing the world's first peace treaty between equals. But none of that happened in isolation. The Hittite king who wrote to the pharaoh as "Brother" was one node in a dense web of trade, diplomacy, and shared technology that tied the whole eastern Mediterranean together. This chapter pauses the royal narrative to take that web apart and see how it actually worked — because understanding it is the only way to understand why, in the next chapter, it all comes crashing down at once.
setup: This chapter explains the machinery of the Late Bronze Age world, starting from a single sunken ship. Around 1300 BCE a merchant vessel went down off the Turkish coast at Uluburun carrying cargo from at least seven cultures — ten tons of Cypriot copper, a ton of Afghan tin, Baltic amber, a gold scarab of Nefertiti — a floating cross-section of an interconnected economy. Three things held that world together: long-distance trade (especially the scarce tin that bronze required), cuneiform as a shared diplomatic language every great king wrote in, and the chariot as the universal, expensive weapon only wealthy states could afford. The Hittites controlled key tin routes and contributed their own innovations — the heavy three-man chariot, the oldest surviving horse-training manual, a law code that favored restitution over an-eye-for-an-eye, and emerging iron-smelting techniques the king guarded like a state secret. The point of all this detail is a setup: this system was strong precisely because it was interconnected, and that same interconnection was about to become the thing that killed it.

bridge: Chapter 6 laid out the interconnected machinery of the Late Bronze Age — the trade in scarce tin, the shared cuneiform diplomacy, the chariot armies, the mobile expertise — and ended on a warning: a system this interdependent is only as strong as its weakest links. The Hittites sat near the center of it, controlling tin routes and corresponding with Egypt as an equal, their world seemingly permanent. Around 1200 BCE, in the span of roughly fifty years, that entire world stops working.
setup: This chapter is the end — and the central mystery of the whole narrative, because the Hittites don't just decline, they vanish more completely than any other major civilization in ancient history. The traditional villain is the Sea Peoples, the mysterious coalition of raiders the Egyptians recorded fighting off, but who they actually were nobody can say for sure, and blaming them alone is too simple. The modern understanding is a systems collapse: a death spiral of mutually reinforcing crises — a decades-long drought that hit the marginal Anatolian plateau hardest (the king's own letters beg Egypt for emergency grain), trade routes seizing up, internal rivalry between Hattusa and the alternate capital at Tarhuntassa, earthquakes, and raiders — each failure feeding the next until no single state could break out. The last known Hittite king wins a sea battle off Cyprus even as the empire crumbles. Around 1178 BCE Hattusa is deliberately burned and never rebuilt. What this chapter has to answer is the hardest question in the book: why did the Hittites, alone among the great powers, disappear so utterly that the world forgot they had ever existed?

bridge: Chapter 7 ended with Hattusa burned around 1178 BCE, the empire gone, and a civilization sliding toward a three-thousand-year silence so total that its very existence would be forgotten. The great Bronze Age world — the trade routes, the brotherhood of Great Kings, the cuneiform diplomacy — had collapsed all at once. But "forgotten" is not the same as "vanished without trace." In the wreckage of the empire's southern and southeastern lands, fragments of the Hittite world kept going, and those fragments are the thread that eventually leads back to the modern day.
setup: This chapter is the long afterlife and the detective story of rediscovery. For five centuries after Hattusa fell, small Neo-Hittite states in Syria and southeastern Anatolia — led by Carchemish, whose royal line descended from Suppiluliuma I — preserved Hittite art, titles, and a hieroglyphic script in the Luwian language, surviving in a poorer, fragmented world until the Neo-Assyrian Empire swallowed them one by one, the last falling by 700 BCE. Then comes the silence. The story of how the empire came back begins not at Hattusa but with carved stones nobody could read, an 1887 cache of letters from a peasant's garden in Egypt mentioning a forgotten land called "Hatti," Hugo Winckler's 1906 dig at Boğazköy that turned up a copy of the very peace treaty from Chapter 5, and finally a Czech linguist, Bedřich Hrozný, who in 1915 noticed that the Hittite words for "eat" and "water" sounded like Latin, English, and German. What's at stake here is the whole point of the book: how a world-historic civilization could be erased so thoroughly, and how it was pulled back out of the ground.
